items.question: Give an account of the Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE) between Alexander and Porus, highlighting the tactics used and its significance.
items.modelAnswer: The **Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE)** was fought on the banks of the **Jhelum (Hydaspes) river** between **Alexander** and **King Porus** of the **Paurava kingdom**, which lay between the **Jhelum and Chenab**. Alexander led a **seasoned Macedonian army** of cavalry, infantry, archers and siege weapons; Porus fielded a **well-equipped Indian army** with a formidable **elephant corps**. The **river was in full flood**, so Alexander used **deception** — feigning movements along the bank by day, then **secretly crossing upstream at night** at an unprotected spot. In battle, Porus massed his **elephants** at the front, but the Macedonians **outflanked** them and harassed them with **javelins and arrows**, causing the panicked elephants to **trample Porus's own troops**. Porus was **defeated and captured**, yet his bravery so impressed Alexander that, on the reply **"Treat me like a king,"** Alexander **restored his kingdom** and made him a **vassal**. The battle was a **turning point** demonstrating Alexander's tactical brilliance, but it was a **costly victory** that left his army exhausted and unwilling to advance — soon leading to the mutiny at the Beas.
keyPoints: 326 BCE, on the flooded Jhelum (Hydaspes); Alexander vs Porus of Paurava.
Alexander's disciplined army vs Porus's war-elephant corps.
Deception: feigned movements by day, secret upstream night crossing.
Macedonians outflanked elephants; javelins/arrows panicked them onto Porus's own troops.
Porus captured but restored as a vassal ('Treat me like a king'); costly turning-point victory.

items.question: Assess the impact of Alexander's invasion on India, and explain why it serves as an important chronological anchor for early Indian history.
items.modelAnswer: Although Alexander's Indian campaign (**327–325 BCE**) was **brief**, its impact was considerable. Culturally, it facilitated the spread of **Hellenistic influence** in **art, architecture and coinage**, and the founding of cities such as **Alexandria on the Indus** and **Alexandria Bucephala**. The **Indo-Greek cultural exchange** had long-lasting effects, especially in **North-West India**, shaping the later **Indo-Greek Kingdoms**. The campaign also **opened land routes** and sustained **Indo-Greek contact** between India and the Hellenistic world. Politically, Alexander's **early departure** and the **establishment of Greek satrapies** could not survive the vacuum: local rulers reasserted control, and the fragmentation cleared the path for the **Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya**. Finally, because Alexander's campaign and his **death in 323 BCE** are firmly dated in Greek sources, they provide one of the **firmest fixed points** in early Indian chronology, helping historians anchor the otherwise fluid dating of the Mauryan rise.
keyPoints: Spread of Hellenistic influence in art, architecture, coinage; new cities (Bucephala, Alexandria-on-Indus).
Indo-Greek cultural exchange shaped North-West India and later Indo-Greek Kingdoms.
Opened land trade routes and sustained Indo-Greek contact.
Greek satrapies collapsed; vacuum enabled Chandragupta's Mauryan Empire.
Firmly dated campaign (327–325 BCE) and death (323 BCE) anchor early Indian chronology.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Invasion of Alexander (Impact of Alexander's Indian Campaign); standard chronology (death 323 BCE)

items.question: Trace the background and causes of Alexander's invasion of India and the route his army followed into the subcontinent.
items.modelAnswer: Alexander inherited a powerful base from his father **Philip II of Macedonia**, who had reformed the army around the **phalanx** and **sarissa**, subdued Greece at **Chaeronea (338 BCE)**, and formed the **League of Corinth**. Ascending the throne in **336 BCE** at the age of 20 and educated by **Aristotle**, Alexander embarked on world conquest. Having **conquered Persia** and defeated **Darius III**, he was drawn eastward by the **riches and fertile lands of India** and by **reports of the wealth** of its kingdoms; the Greeks already knew of India through the **Persian Empire**, which held territory in present-day **Pakistan and Afghanistan**. His army crossed the **Hindu Kush** into **Bactria**, passed through **Gandhara**, and entered the **Punjab (327–325 BCE)**. There **Ambhi of Taxila submitted without a fight** and became an ally, supplying troops and provisions, while the strongest resistance awaited at the Jhelum in the person of **Porus**.
keyPoints: Base built by Philip II: phalanx/sarissa, Chaeronea (338 BCE), League of Corinth.
Alexander crowned 336 BCE (aged 20), tutored by Aristotle.
Causes: India's riches/fertile lands, reports of wealth; prior Greek knowledge via Persia.
Route: Hindu Kush → Bactria → Gandhara → Punjab (327–325 BCE).
Ambhi of Taxila submitted and allied; Porus posed the main resistance at the Jhelum.
